summary: Defines RPSL, a language operators use to describe routing policies, such as which networks they accept routes from and announce to, in the Internet Routing Registry. The policies can be detailed enough to help generate router configurations. It replaced RFC 2280.

plainLanguage.summary: RPSL is a text format for recording how networks exchange route information. Its structured objects can help people inspect routing rules and can provide input for generating router configurations.

questions: how do import and export work in rpsl
subtitle: A shared language for recording which routes networks accept, announce, and prefer.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a shared, precise way to record routing policies and the information needed to check or generate router configurations. Earlier policy languages could not express some policies.
tldr.mechanism: RPSL stores policy and network facts in named objects. An AS object describes import and export rules, while route, set, router, and dictionary objects supply related information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2622 replaced RFC 2280. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 4012 and RFC 7909.

sections.title: What RPSL Describes
sections.content:
The Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) lets network operators describe routing policy at different levels, including the Autonomous System (AS) level. It can express enough detail for low-level router configurations to be generated from the policy.

RPSL is a language for describing policy, not a router configuration language. The RFC describes a goal of keeping a view of global routing policy in a cooperatively maintained, distributed database. The registry's process for registering objects is outside this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: RPSL records the rules a network uses when exchanging routes with other networks. Tools can use these records to help check policy or prepare router settings.

sections.title: The Shape of an RPSL Object
sections.content:
An RPSL object is a text list of attribute and value pairs, with one pair on each line. The attribute starts at the beginning of the line and is followed by a colon; a blank line ends the object. Continuation lines start with a space, tab, or plus sign, and a hash mark starts a comment.

RPSL is case-insensitive and uses ASCII characters. Each object has a key made from one or more attributes. Attributes can be required or optional, and can have one or several values. Address-prefix range operators select more-specific prefixes, with rules that define how those ranges combine.
sections.plainLanguage: An RPSL object is a small text record with one named fact on each line. Its class and key identify what the record describes, while a blank line marks its end.

sections.title: People, Routes, and Reusable Sets
sections.content:
A mntner object records authentication information for requests to create, delete, or update maintained objects. person and role objects hold contact details; a role can remain the same when the people performing it change.

A route object records an address prefix and the AS that originates it. Those two values form its key, so the same prefix originated by different ASes has distinct route objects. Named sets collect ASes, routes, routers, filters, or peerings; their members can be listed directly or included by reference under specified maintainer rules.

Filters select routes using address prefixes, AS paths, route sets, and routing attributes. They can combine conditions with AND, OR, and NOT, which lets a policy refer to a group of routes instead of listing each one separately.
sections.plainLanguage: RPSL records contacts, route origins, and groups of related networks or routers. A policy can name one of these groups and apply a filter to decide which routes match.

sections.title: Import and Export Policy
sections.content:
An aut-num object describes an AS. Its import attributes say which routes the AS accepts from specified peerings; its export attributes say which routes it announces to them. Optional actions can set or change route attributes, and multiple actions in one expression run from left to right.

Several statements can cover the same peering or routes. RPSL resolves this using the specification-order rule: the first applicable statement takes precedence for the routes it covers. The default attribute describes a peer or router to use for default routing, optionally restricted by a filter.

Optional protocol and into clauses describe policies for other protocols or route injection between protocols. The RFC also defines structured import and export expressions using except and refine, and recommends these for advanced users.
sections.plainLanguage: Import rules say what an AS accepts from its neighbors, and export rules say what it announces to them. If rules overlap, RPSL applies the earlier matching rule first.

sections.title: The Dictionary and Compatible Extensions
sections.content:
The dictionary class makes RPSL extensible. Dictionary objects define routing-policy attributes, types, and protocols, and tools use the well-known dictionary named RPSL by default. The RFC's initial dictionary includes attributes such as pref, med, aspath, and community.

The RFC prefers extending the dictionary first, then adding attributes to existing classes, then adding classes. Changing the syntax of existing attributes is a last resort. Extensions should preserve compatibility, and tools are expected to ignore attributes they do not understand.
sections.plainLanguage: The dictionary defines the policy terms and protocol options that tools can recognize. New definitions can extend the language while older tools ignore unfamiliar attributes.

sections.title: Aggregates, Static Routes, and Routers
sections.content:
Route objects can describe aggregate routes, which summarize more-specific routes. Their attributes specify component routes, where aggregation happens, and which more-specific routes may still be exported. Outside the aggregation boundary, only the aggregate is exported by default; route and AS export policies also determine what is allowed.

The inject attribute can describe which routers generate an aggregate and the conditions for doing so. With upon static, it can also describe static routes and actions such as setting a next hop or cost. An inet-rtr object records a router's name, local AS, interface addresses, and peerings.
sections.plainLanguage: An aggregate replaces several detailed routes with a broader route for networks outside the aggregation boundary. RPSL can also record the routers and conditions involved, plus static routes that a router injects.

sections.title: Security and Object Control
sections.content:
The mntner class identifies who controls maintained RPSL objects. Its auth attribute names authentication methods for update requests, including NONE, MAIL-FROM, PGP-KEY, and CRYPT-PW.

The protocols used by routing registries to exchange RPSL objects are outside this document's scope. The RFC expects those systems to use suitable security techniques, naming IPsec, TLS, and PGP/MIME as examples.
sections.plainLanguage: A maintainer object records how update requests for database objects are authenticated. The RFC leaves the communication protocols to registries and says they should use suitable security methods.
